summary: Gives hints and recommendations so an IMAP4 implementation can work with older IMAP2 and IMAP2bis implementations. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1732 collects suggestions for making IMAP4 software work with older IMAP2 and IMAP2bis software. It explains how to detect older servers, choose substitute commands, and avoid several known compatibility problems.

questions: how to detect an imap2 server
subtitle: Hints for IMAP4 clients and servers that need to communicate with older IMAP2 software.

tldr.problem: IMAP4 was designed to be compatible with earlier versions, but older IMAP2 and IMAP2bis clients and servers may lack newer commands or behave differently.
tldr.mechanism: The memo suggests checking server capabilities, trying fallback commands, and accounting for known differences between older clients and IMAP4 servers.
tldr.outcome: These are optional implementation hints, not requirements of the IMAP4 specification. RFC 1732 is an Informational memo about compatibility as understood in 1994.

today: RFC 1732 is an Informational memo, and the unit metadata lists no RFC as obsoleting or updating it. Its compatibility advice reflects the IMAP implementations discussed in December 1994.

sections.title: Purpose of the Compatibility Hints
sections.content:
This memo summarizes hints and recommendations for IMAP4 implementations that need to interoperate with earlier specifications. The IMAP4 specification does not require these hints; implementers decide whether they want their software to fail when it meets older software. The author also warns that the list may be incomplete and reflects current implementation knowledge and experience.

IMAP4 was designed so that features absent from earlier specifications would usually remain invisible unless a client requested them. Some older servers may also support newer facilities as experimental IMAP2 extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo offers optional ways to work with older IMAP software. It is a collection of implementation advice, not a set of required IMAP4 rules.

sections.title: Finding Older Servers and Choosing Fallbacks
sections.content:
A client can try the CAPABILITY command to check for IMAP4 support. An OK response that includes IMAP4 indicates an IMAP4 server; a BAD response or one without that capability indicates an older server. For facilities without this check, the client may try a command and treat a BAD response as evidence that the server lacks it.

The memo lists substitutes for many newer facilities. Examples include using LOGIN instead of AUTHENTICATE, SELECT instead of EXAMINE, and the older FIND command instead of LIST and LSUB. Some IMAP4 facilities, including UID commands and the UID fetch item, have no older equivalent. The memo also advises clients to accept all response and data formats documented for IMAP4 and not depend on server extensions outside its base specification.
sections.plainLanguage: A client can ask what the server supports, then use an older command when the newer one is missing. Some newer features have no substitute, so an old server cannot provide them.

sections.title: Differences That Affect Older Clients
sections.content:
The memo says a conforming IMAP4 server should generally work with a well-written client for an earlier specification, but it lists known differences. Older wording led some clients to expect CHECK to return the current message count; the memo says clients should instead remember the latest EXISTS response and avoid unnecessary CHECK commands. Unlike older behavior, IMAP4 COPY does not automatically create a missing destination mailbox.

Other differences include the date and time format, which may use a four-digit year and a signed four-digit time zone, and the handling of backslashes in quoted strings. The memo recommends literals instead of quoted strings when the string contains a backslash or double quote. It also notes that old servers may differ in mailbox creation and preservation of flags or internal dates during COPY.
sections.plainLanguage: Older clients may expect a message count from CHECK or a mailbox to be created by COPY. They may also fail to parse newer date formats or quoted strings, so implementers need to account for these differences.
